title: Role and Record of the UN

cards.h: Eighty years of the world's parliament
cards.b:
The United Nations was founded in 1945 "to save succeeding generations from the scourge of war", in the words of the Charter's preamble. It turned 80 in 2025, in a year of war in Ukraine, Gaza and Sudan, deep budget cuts and a reform drive called UN80.

UPSC asks you to assess its role and record: peace and security, development, human rights, decolonisation. Answers need balance. The UN failed in Rwanda and is blocked over Ukraine, yet it feeds millions, runs peace operations and sets global norms.

Learn the Charter's purposes and organs, key articles, landmark successes and failures, and India's contribution. The reform side is in the next lesson.

• Atlantic Charter (August 1941): Roosevelt and Churchill's war aims.
  • Declaration by United Nations (1 January 1942): 26 Allied states, India among them.
  • Dumbarton Oaks (1944) drafted the structure; Yalta (February 1945) agreed the veto.
  • San Francisco Conference (April-June 1945): 50 states signed the Charter on 26 June 1945. Poland signed later as the 51st original member.
  • The Charter entered into force on 24 October 1945, now UN Day.

India, then under British rule, was an original member. Membership today is 193 states, with South Sudan (2011) the newest. Palestine and the Holy See are non-member observer states.

Purposes (Article 1)

Maintain peace and security; develop friendly relations based on equal rights and self-determination; cooperate on economic, social, cultural and humanitarian problems and human rights; be a centre for harmonising actions.

Key principles (Article 2)

Sovereign equality; peaceful settlement of disputes; Article 2(4): no threat or use of force against the territorial integrity or political independence of any state; Article 2(7): no intervention in domestic matters, except Chapter VII enforcement.

Six principal organs

General Assembly, Security Council, Economic and Social Council (ECOSOC), Trusteeship Council (suspended since 1994 after Palau), International Court of Justice (The Hague), Secretariat (led by the Secretary-General).

The P5 are China, France, Russia, the UK and the US. The Council grew from 11 to 15 members in 1965. The veto has been used most by the USSR/Russia and the US.

The Assembly controls the budget, elects non-permanent members, and with the Council appoints the Secretary-General and ICJ judges. The Uniting for Peace resolution (1950) lets it act when a veto blocks the Council. Since 2022, a General Assembly debate must follow every veto (resolution 76/262).

The Secretary-General is the "chief administrative officer" (Article 97), appointed by the General Assembly on the Council's recommendation, for five years by convention, renewable. Article 99 lets the SG bring threats to peace to the Council's attention, a power Antonio Guterres used on Gaza in December 2023.

  • Trygve Lie, Dag Hammarskjold (died in 1961 in a plane crash in Africa), U Thant, Kurt Waldheim, Javier Perez de Cuellar, Boutros Boutros-Ghali (An Agenda for Peace, 1992), Kofi Annan (Nobel 2001), Ban Ki-moon, and Antonio Guterres (2017-2026).
  • Guterres's term ends on 31 December 2026. The 2026 selection used public candidate dialogues and Council straw polls. Women's groups pushed for the first woman SG. As of November 2026 the Council had held several straw polls but not yet made a recommendation. Guterres's term ends on 31 December 2026.

Hammarskjold shaped "preventive diplomacy" and peacekeeping. Critics say the SG is "more secretary than general", dependent on the P5.

Successes or partial successes

  • Korea (1950) and the reversal of Iraq's invasion of Kuwait (1990-91).
  • Suez (1956): the first armed peacekeeping force, UNEF.
  • Missions that helped end wars in Namibia (1989-90), Mozambique, El Salvador, Cambodia (UNTAC, 1992-93), Sierra Leone, Liberia and Timor-Leste.
  • No third world war; nuclear and chemical arms treaties negotiated under UN auspices.

Failures

  • Paralysis during much of the Cold War.
  • Rwanda (1994): troops were cut while about 800,000 people were killed. Srebrenica (1995).
  • Iraq (2003): war without Council approval.
  • Syria (from 2011), Ukraine (from 2022), Gaza (from 2023) and Sudan: vetoes or weak responses.

Peacekeeping: over 70 operations since 1948. The Blue Helmets won the Nobel Peace Prize in 1988.

cards.h: Beyond security: development, rights and norms
cards.b:
• Decolonisation. The 1960 Declaration (resolution 1514) helped about 80 former colonies join. Membership rose from 51 to 193.
  • Human rights. UDHR (1948), the covenants (1966), CEDAW, the Human Rights Council (2006).
  • Development. UNDP, UNCTAD, the Millennium Development Goals (2000-15) and the Sustainable Development Goals (2015-30), 17 goals.
  • Humanitarian work. WFP (Nobel 2020), UNHCR (Nobel 1954 and 1981), UNICEF (Nobel 1965).
  • Environment. Stockholm (1972), UNFCCC (1992), Paris Agreement (2015).
  • Law. UNCLOS (1982), the ICJ, international criminal tribunals.
  • Pact for the Future (September 2024): commitments on Council reform, digital cooperation and future generations.

Many scholars say the UN's quiet, everyday work matters more than its high-politics failures.

Realists

The UN reflects great-power interests; it works only when the P5 agree. Morgenthau and Mearsheimer doubt that it constrains states.

Liberals

It lowers transaction costs, spreads information and builds habits of cooperation. Imperfect, but better than none.

Constructivists

It creates and spreads norms: sovereignty, decolonisation, human rights, R2P (Finnemore).

Critical and Global South views

The veto and the P5 freeze the power map of 1945. Funding by a few rich states shapes priorities.

Inis Claude, Swords into Plowshares (1956), and Paul Kennedy, The Parliament of Man (2006), are standard histories.

• Money. The UN faces a liquidity crisis. The US, which pays about 22% of the regular budget, cut contributions sharply. The 2026 regular budget was cut to $3.45 billion (adopted December 2025, about 15% below 2025), and thousands of posts were cut.
  • Retreat of a founder. The US left WHO, the Paris Agreement and the Human Rights Council, and announced it will leave UNESCO from 31 December 2026, and in January 2026 announced exits from 66 international bodies, 31 of them UN-linked.
  • Council deadlock. Vetoes on Ukraine and Gaza; little action on Sudan.
  • Wars of 2026. Conflict involving Iran, Israel and the US from February 2026 bypassed the Council.
  • Legitimacy. The South asks why Africa and India have no permanent seat.

The UN80 Initiative (launched March 2025) aims to cut costs, review mandates and merge bodies. See the next lesson.

• Founding member. India signed the 1942 Declaration and the 1945 Charter.
  • Human rights and decolonisation. Hansa Mehta in UDHR drafting; India raised apartheid in 1946.
  • Kashmir. India took the issue to the Council in January 1948; it now insists on bilateralism (Simla Agreement, 1972).
  • Peacekeeping. One of the largest troop contributors since the 1950s (Korea, Congo, Gaza, Lebanon, South Sudan), with the first all-women police unit (Liberia, 2007).
  • Security Council. Elected eight times, most recently for 2021-22. India seeks a permanent seat, working with the G4.
  • Leadership. Vijaya Lakshmi Pandit was the first woman President of the General Assembly (1953).
  • Norms. International Day of Yoga (2014), the International Year of Millets (2023), and India's CCIT proposal (1996).

"Evaluate the role of the UN in maintaining international peace and security."
"The UN has failed but it is indispensable." Discuss.
"Discuss India's contribution to the United Nations."

Structure: founding and purposes (Articles 1, 2(4), 2(7)); organs with the Council and Assembly diagram; Secretary-General's role (Articles 97, 99). Record: peace successes and failures, then development, rights, decolonisation and environment. Theories in brief. Current crisis (funding, US exits, vetoes, UN80). India's role. Conclusion: reform, not abandonment.

quiz.q: The UN Charter came into force on:

o: The threat or use of force against states

quiz.q: The Security Council was enlarged from 11 to 15 members in:
quiz.w: By an amendment that came into force in 1965.

quiz.q: Which Charter article allows the Secretary-General to bring a threat to the Council's attention?
quiz.w: Guterres invoked it on Gaza in December 2023.

quiz.q: Since 2022, a General Assembly debate must be held whenever:
o: A veto is cast in the Security Council

quiz.q: The Trusteeship Council suspended operations after the independence of:
quiz.w: Palau, the last trust territory, became independent in 1994.

quiz.q: UN peacekeepers won the Nobel Peace Prize in:
quiz.w: The 2020 prize went to the WFP; Kofi Annan and the UN won in 2001.

quiz.q: Who was the first woman President of the UN General Assembly?

quiz.w: It set out preventive diplomacy, peacemaking, peacekeeping and peacebuilding.

quiz.q: The UN80 Initiative was launched in:
quiz.w: To cut costs, review mandates and restructure.
